body:
Priya Raman: Thanks for joining, Dr. Whitaker, Alicia. I know your schedule is tight so let's jump in. Elena from our product team is here specifically to talk through the HIPAA question.

Dr. James Whitaker: Appreciated. Look, we love the product in the demo environment. The latency is impressive — under seven hundred milliseconds, which is honestly better than what we're getting from our current IVR vendor. But we cannot go live until we have a fully executed BAA and end-to-end HIPAA compliance documentation.

Alicia Park: Right, and to be specific — we need to see how PHI is handled at every hop. Transcription, storage, the LLM calls, the analytics pipeline. Our security review board is going to ask about each of those.

Elena Sokolova: Understood. Let me be straightforward about where we are. Voice_agent_v1 is not HIPAA compliant today. We do not offer a BAA on v1. Voice_agent_v2, which goes GA in November, will be HIPAA compliant — we've been working with a healthcare-focused security firm since May and we're in the final audit phase.

Dr. James Whitaker: November. That's tight for us. Our fiscal year starts January and we've earmarked budget for this.

Elena Sokolova: What v2 gives you specifically — private-tenant transcription with no data retention outside the BAA scope, zero data used for model training, encrypted storage with customer-managed keys, and audit logs on every PHI touch. We'll also sign the BAA directly.

Alicia Park: What about the LLM inference itself? Are you routing to OpenAI or Anthropic on the backend?

Elena Sokolova: On v2 we've got a BAA-covered path through both providers. So the inference layer is included in our BAA. On v1 that's not the case, which is why v1 isn't compliant.

Dr. James Whitaker: Okay. That answers the technical piece. What about pediatric use cases — we have a large pediatric line and there's a whole additional layer with parental consent and minor's PHI.

Alicia Park: We'd need the system to detect when the caller is speaking on behalf of a minor and route those calls through a different consent flow.

Elena Sokolova: That's not in the v2 launch scope. That's a specific feature we'd need to design. Can you send me the exact requirements? If it's on the roadmap for Q1 of twenty-twenty-six I think we could commit to it.

Dr. James Whitaker: I'll have my team put together a spec. But we need it — this isn't a nice-to-have, this is a launch blocker for the pediatric line.

Priya Raman: Let me make sure I'm capturing this right. Nimbus needs — one, v2 GA with BAA, target November. Two, pediatric consent routing feature, target Q1 twenty-twenty-six. Three, everything documented for your security board review.

Alicia Park: Correct. And I'll add — we need Spanish language support at some point but that's a phase two thing, not a blocker for signing.

Elena Sokolova: Noted. Spanish is on the roadmap for Q2. I'll flag it in the deal notes.

Dr. James Whitaker: What are we looking at in terms of contract value if we sign for the full pediatric plus adult volume?

Priya Raman: Enterprise tier, and given your call volume — you said around ninety thousand a month across both lines — I'd estimate somewhere between four-fifty and five-fifty a year on a two-year term. I can firm that up once we scope the pediatric feature.

Dr. James Whitaker: Alright. Elena, send us the v2 security whitepaper, the draft BAA, and a technical spec template for the pediatric consent routing. Alicia, you'll drive the security review from our side.

Alicia Park: On it.

Priya Raman: A couple of practical questions before we wrap. Where are your call recordings currently stored?

Alicia Park: Right now they're in an on-prem system that our contact center vendor manages. We've been trying to migrate to cloud for two years.

Elena Sokolova: With v2 we'd store them in an encrypted S3 bucket in a segregated tenant just for Nimbus. You'd have the encryption keys. If you want on-prem-style controls we can also offer a bring-your-own-bucket option.

Alicia Park: Bring-your-own-bucket is interesting. Send docs on that.

Dr. James Whitaker: What about integration with Epic? We use Epic for our EHR and our patient identity is tied to Epic MRNs.

Elena Sokolova: We have an Epic connector for demographic lookup. Not for clinical data — that's out of scope. But for identity verification on inbound calls, yes, we can hit Epic's Interconnect API.

Dr. James Whitaker: Good. That's what I'd need.

Priya Raman: One process thing — do you need to do a HIPAA risk assessment as part of your security review?

Alicia Park: Yes. Our board requires a documented risk assessment for any new vendor touching PHI.

Elena Sokolova: We have a template we've used with two other health systems. I'll include it in the packet.

Dr. James Whitaker: Great, that saves us a lot of work.

Priya Raman: Great. Let's reconvene in three weeks with the pediatric spec and a firm quote.

Dr. James Whitaker: Works. Thanks everyone.

Alicia Park: Thanks all.

Priya Raman: One quick logistics question — how does your procurement process work? Master vendor list, competitive bid, sole source?

Dr. James Whitaker: For a purchase this size, competitive bid, but we can position Voxly as the incumbent given the ongoing pilot.

Alicia Park: We'll need at least two other vendor quotes on file.

Priya Raman: Understood. We can help you scope the RFP if it saves time.

Dr. James Whitaker: That would be useful.

Elena Sokolova: I can also send a technical requirements template you can lift into your RFP.

Alicia Park: Perfect.

Dr. James Whitaker: Alright, we're at time. Thanks everyone.

Elena Sokolova: Thanks for the great discussion.
